strengths: Identifies and clearly documents an important, previously overlooked limitation of text-conditioned VAR models (severe lack of per-prompt diversity), which is a valuable empirical finding for the community given the rapid adoption of VAR architectures.

Scale-travel is a genuinely novel and well-motivated inference-time mechanism: the analogy between diffusion time-travel and VAR's scale-wise structure is intuitive, and re-encoding an intermediate feature map Z_l with the multi-scale VQ encoder to 'rewind' to a coarser scale is a clever, training-free solution that is specific to VAR's architecture.

The evaluation is thorough: Pareto-frontier analysis across two datasets (MS-COCO, MJHQ-30K) and two VAR models (Infinity, Switti), multiple diversity metrics (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi, SSCD-based) and quality metrics (ImageReward, FID), plus systematic baselines (CFG scheduling variants, condition-annealing on text embedding vs. <SOS>, temperature, top-p, prompt-rewriting).

The supplementary is substantive: scheduler ablations, scale-travel hyperparameter sweeps (l, m), inference-time measurements showing modest ~15-24% overhead, and text-alignment checks (GenEval, VQAScore) that anticipate the natural objection that diversity gains might harm prompt fidelity.

Training-free and model-agnostic across two VAR backbones, which increases the practical significance and reproducibility of the approach; limitations (residual ~6% artifact rate, slightly higher inference cost) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Overall novelty is moderate. The first stage (noise injection into the text embedding) is a direct port of CADS [55] to VAR, and scale-travel, while new for VAR, is explicitly an adaptation of the well-established time-travel idea from diffusion models. The core algorithmic change is small (the authors themselves note it is 'a minor change' to multi-scale encoding), which limits the depth of the methodological contribution.

The method does not fully resolve the quality-diversity trade-off: Table 1 shows a persistent ~11% ImageReward drop relative to the base model for Infinity (1.22 -> 1.08), and the paper concedes ~6% of samples still contain visual artifacts. The contribution is a better Pareto point rather than an elimination of the trade-off.

Evidence quality has gaps: FID is computed from only 10K generated images (1000 prompts x 10), which is small and noisy for FID estimation; evaluation relies on automated metrics (ImageReward, LPIPS-MPD) that may not fully capture the visual artifacts shown qualitatively; no human evaluation is provided.

Text-alignment degradation is non-trivial for Switti (GenEval 0.615 -> 0.586, with a large drop in counting 0.544 -> 0.494 and position 0.118 -> 0.128), and the paper's framing that alignment 'does not significantly degrade' understates this; the mechanistic explanation is largely hypothetical.

Key design choices appear empirically rather than analytically grounded: the choice of refinement start scale l=8, target scale m, and the noise schedules are tuned per model via hyperparameter search on the evaluation benchmarks, raising mild concerns about generalization and about selection of hyperparameters on test data.

The claim of being 'first to systematically increase the diversity of VAR models' is asserted rather than rigorously substantiated against all concurrent VAR work (e.g., temperature/randomized-order variants are only partially compared).

strengths: Identifies and systematically studies an underexplored and practically relevant problem: the lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned VAR models, which the paper convincingly demonstrates and motivates (Fig. 1, Sec. 3).
The proposed pipeline is training-free, requires no fine-tuning, and adds only modest inference overhead (~15-24% per the supplementary), which is appealing for practical deployment.

Scale-travel is a clever, VAR-specific analog of diffusion 'time-travel': reusing the multi-scale autoencoder to rewind an intermediate latent to a coarser scale and resume generation is a neat exploitation of the next-scale structure, and the pseudocode comparison (Fig. 4) makes the mechanism transparent.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: two VAR backbones (Infinity, Switti), two benchmarks (MS-COCO, MJHQ-30K), Pareto-front analyses across multiple diversity/quality metrics, ablations over schedulers, CFG weights, temperature/top-p, scale-travel parameters (l, m), text-alignment checks (GenEval, VQAScore), and a comparison against prompt-rewriting.

The paper is generally well organized, with background on next-scale prediction that makes the method accessible, and an honest limitations statement (residual artifacts in ~6% of samples, extra inference cost).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: both components are direct adaptations of existing diffusion-model techniques. Text-embedding noise injection is essentially CADS [55] ported to VAR, and scale-travel is a small modification of the already-existing multi-scale encoder (Alg. 2 vs Alg. 1 differ in one line: encoding Z_l instead of Z). The contribution is more an application/transplant of known ideas than a new algorithmic insight.

The quality cost of the method is not fully resolved: relative to the default VAR models, DiverseVAR still trades a noticeable drop in ImageReward (−11.5% on Infinity/MJHQ, −16% on Switti/MJHQ) and in GenEval/VQAScore for its diversity gains, and 6% of samples still exhibit visual artifacts. The claimed 'sweet spot' is therefore partial rather than a clear Pareto improvement over simply tuning sampling hyperparameters in some regimes.

Evidence of the Pareto-front superiority is somewhat fragile: Fig. 6 curves are based on only 100 prompts (10 images each) for the front tracing, show non-monotonic and noisy behavior for several baselines, and the metric suite (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi, SSCD) can conflate diversity with quality degradation. No human evaluation is provided to verify that the diversity gains are perceptually meaningful and that residual artifacts are acceptable.

Internal inconsistencies weaken confidence: the supplementary (Sec. B) concludes 'we adopt the constant scheduler for our main experiments,' while Sec. D and the main text state a cosine scheduler for condition-annealing; there are also typos ('VARs models', 'simliar') and ambiguous statements about which component contributes the diversity vs. the quality recovery (the role of scale-travel alone vs. annealing alone is not cleanly isolated in Tab. 1).

The choice of the refinement start scale (l=8) and target scale (m=3/4) is justified only empirically via a small grid search on the evaluation benchmarks, raising concerns about hyperparameter tuning on test data and about generalization to other VAR models or resolutions.

The key enabling assumption—that multi-scale encoding of an intermediate feature map Z_l yields coarse tokens semantically equivalent to those of the full latent (Fig. A.2)—is supported only by qualitative visualization, not by any quantitative analysis of reconstruction fidelity or failure modes when the assumption breaks.

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates an underexplored problem: the lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned VAR models (Infinity, Switti), which has received far less attention than quality in this emerging model family.

Scale-Travel is a clean, VAR-specific contribution: the insight that the multi-scale autoencoder enables approximate 'rewinding' of the autoregressive process (re-encoding an intermediate feature map and discarding fine scales) is simple, elegant, and genuinely novel relative to diffusion-style time-travel, which is shown to be inapplicable to VAR.
The method is training-free and inference-time only, with modest overhead quantified in the supplementary (~15–24% on an RTX 3090), making it practical and widely applicable.

Comprehensive evaluation: Pareto-front analysis across two VAR backbones (Infinity, Switti) and two benchmarks (MS-COCO, MJHQ-30K) with multiple complementary metrics (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi, SSCD, ImageReward, FID), plus extensive supplementary ablations (schedulers, scale-travel parameters l and m, CFG weights, temperature, top-p, prompt-rewriting comparison, GenEval/VQAScore text-alignment checks).

Fair attribution of prior techniques: the paper transparently credits CADS [55] and CFG scheduling [28, 68] for the diversity stage and positions its contribution as the systematic study of these in VAR plus the new refinement mechanism.

Honest limitations section (residual artifacts in ~6% of samples, inference overhead), and the supplementary provides enough detail (pseudocode, hyperparameters, inference times) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is largely incremental: the diversity stage is a direct transfer of diffusion-model techniques (CFG scheduling, CADS noise injection) to VAR, and the refinement stage is an adaptation of time-travel intuitions; the core new element is the re-encoding-based scale-travel, which is a fairly small algorithmic change (Fig. 4 shows only a minor modification of the standard encoder). This is defensible for a training-free method paper, but the work sits closer to an applied/systems contribution than a new algorithmic framework.

Table 1 is ambiguous: rows '+Cond. Anneal.' and '+Scale-Travel' do not make explicit whether '+Scale-Travel' is applied alone or combined with condition-annealing; the text suggests the latter, but the table formatting could mislead and prevents a clean assessment of scale-travel's standalone refinement benefit over the base model.

Reliance on automated metrics without human evaluation: diversity gains are measured via LPIPS-MPD/Vendi/SSCD and quality via ImageReward/FID, and these can disagree (e.g., on Infinity, condition-annealing *improves* FID on MJHQ-30K while collapsing ImageReward, suggesting FID here is dominated by diversity rather than perceptual quality). A small-scale human study on the diversity–quality trade-off would substantially strengthen the Pareto-front claims.

Several technical points are under-explained in the main paper: (i) the interaction between the corrupted (noisy-conditioned) feature map Z_l and the quantizer Q during scale-travel re-encoding—why quantized residuals of an off-manifold latent produce valid coarse tokens—is asserted empirically rather than analyzed; (ii) Eq. (8) conditions fine-scale sampling on both re-encoded coarse tokens and previously generated fine tokens in a way that is not fully specified; (iii) the choice of l=8 is justified only by visual inspection (supplementary).

Evaluation scale is modest for Pareto analysis (100 prompts x 10 images per point), and no statistical uncertainty (confidence intervals) is reported, so fine distinctions between methods on the Pareto front are hard to assess; sample-size sensitivity is not discussed.

The generality of scale-travel beyond Infinity/Switti is untested; it is not clear whether the approach applies to VAR variants with different tokenizations (e.g., continuous-token VARs like VAR-d or Fluid), and the paper does not discuss this scope restriction.

Minor clarity issues: typos ('VARs models', 'eiter metrics', inconsistent capitalization of DiverseVAR in tables), and the assumption that the multi-scale autoencoder's encoder is available at test time should be stated explicitly, since some VAR deployments expose only the decoder.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly articulates an underexplored problem: severe per-prompt diversity limitations in text-conditioned VAR models, which is a timely and practically relevant issue given the rapid adoption of next-scale autoregressive generation.

The proposed scale-travel latent refinement is an elegant and technically sound idea that exploits the multi-scale structure of VAR for approximate scale rollback — a non-trivial design in the autoregressive scale-axis setting, with clear pseudocode (Alg. 1/2) demonstrating it requires only a minor modification of multi-scale encoding.

Evidence is comprehensive and appropriately matched to the claims: Pareto-front analyses across two datasets and two image VARs, quantitative tables, video results on InfinityStar via VBench/VBench-2.0, class-conditioned VAR, ablations on schedulers, scale-travel parameters (l, m), repeated refinement steps, model sizes/resolutions, comparisons against fine-tuning baselines (CSD-VAR, Kaleido), prompt rewriting, and inference-time cost measurements (15–24% overhead).
The method is training-free, requires no model retraining, and its hyperparameters and experimental setup are documented in detail, supporting reproducibility.

Limitations are candidly stated (inference overhead, ~6% of samples still with artifacts), and the discussion of alternative diversity controls (CFG, temperature, nucleus sampling, prompt rewriting) positions the contribution fairly.
weaknesses: The diversity-enhancement stage is largely a direct adaptation of existing diffusion techniques (CADS condition-annealing [68] and CFG scheduling [37,82]) to VAR; the main novelty rests on scale-travel, which is essentially multi-scale re-encoding of intermediate latents. While effective, the conceptual contribution is incremental relative to prior refinement/rollback ideas (SDEdit, RePaint).

The final trade-off still involves a measurable quality loss (e.g., Infinity ImageReward drops from 1.22 to 1.08, and GenEval alignment drops notably for Switti from 0.615 to 0.586), and the claimed 'minimal quality degradation' is partly metric-dependent — FID improvements may partly reflect the train/test domain mismatch (models trained on Midjourney-style data evaluated on MS-COCO).

Diversity and quality are assessed entirely through automatic metrics (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi, ImageReward, FID); no human evaluation is provided to validate that the diversity gains and artifact corrections are perceptually meaningful.

The optimal operating point appears sensitive to multiple coupled hyperparameters (noise scale σ, kmax, l, m) selected via a 'toy experiment' in the supplementary; discussion of how robust these choices are across prompts/domains is limited.

Some quantitative details could confuse readers (e.g., Table 1 reports DiverseVAR results at hyperparameter settings that differ across models in ways that are only documented in the supplementary), and the video evaluation applies DiverseVAR only to the keyframe stage, leaving temporal diversity effects only partially characterized.

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates an underexplored and practically relevant problem: the severe lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned VAR models (Infinity, Switti, InfinityStar), which has largely been overlooked relative to quality-focused work.

Scale-Travel is a genuinely novel and well-motivated mechanism: re-using the multi-scale encoder to rewind an intermediate latent Z_l back to a coarser scale m and resume autoregressive generation is a natural fit for the VAR architecture and is presented cleanly (Fig. 4, Alg. 2) with only a minimal change over standard multi-scale encoding.

Extensive and reasonably convincing empirical evidence: Pareto-frontier analysis across two image models and two benchmarks, video generation on InfinityStar, class-conditioned VAR, ablations over scale-travel parameters (l, m) and schedulers, comparisons against prompt rewriting, temperature/nucleus sampling, and fine-tuning baselines (CSD-VAR, Kaleido), plus runtime overhead analysis (~15-24%).

The method is training-free and generalizes across model sizes and resolutions (Tab. A8), which increases its practical value; limitations (residual artifacts in ~6% of samples, added inference cost) are stated.
Supplementary material is thorough, with scheduler details, text-alignment checks (GenEval/VQAScore), and extensive qualitative results.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty in the first stage: condition-annealing via text-embedding noise injection is a direct transfer of CADS [68] to VAR, and CFG scheduling baselines are also borrowed from diffusion literature; the main insight (noise in text embedding works best) is an empirical observation rather than a new technique.

Scale-Travel, while elegant, is essentially an SDEdit/RePaint-style 'rewind and resample' applied along the scale axis of an existing architecture; the resulting diversity-quality trade-off is still substantially worse than the base model's quality (e.g., ImageReward drops from 1.22 to 1.08 on Infinity, 1.18 to 1.05 on Switti; GenEval text-alignment degrades noticeably, e.g., Switti 0.615 to 0.586), so the 'minimal quality degradation' framing is somewhat optimistic.

No human evaluation or user study to substantiate the diversity gains and perceptual quality of DiverseVAR; all conclusions rest on automatic metrics (LPIPS-MPD, Vendi, FID, ImageReward) whose reliability for diversity-quality trade-offs is debatable.

The claimed novelty of 'first to systematically increase diversity of VAR models' should be tempered by the fact that the core mechanisms are adapted; the paper's contribution is more of an applied/systematization nature than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Some experimental details raise questions: FID is computed on only 1000 prompts per method, which is small for reliable FID estimates; several key design choices (l=8, scheduler types) appear selected on the same benchmarks used for evaluation rather than a held-out set; Eq. (6)'s conditioning on r_{m+1},...,r_{k-1} from the original trajectory is not clearly explained.

Presentation issues: the 'Project page' field is empty, there are typos (e.g., '+80.4\%' escaping artifact), and Fig. A2/A3 descriptions are dense; hyperparameters (k_max, sigma, l, m) differ per model, which complicates reproducibility and suggests per-model tuning.

Impact on conditional fidelity under high-diversity settings: the diversity-enhancing configurations reportedly still produce artifacts in ~6% of samples and text alignment drops (color attribution 0.603→0.528 on Infinity), yet no mechanism is proposed to detect or mitigate failure cases at inference time.

strengths: Identifies and clearly documents an under-explored and practically important problem: the severe lack of per-prompt diversity in text-conditioned VAR models, a limitation that has been overshadowed by the field's focus on image quality (Fig. 1 is a convincing motivating example).

The proposed two-stage framework is simple, training-free, and well-motivated. The scale-travel latent refinement is an elegant and novel exploitation of the multi-scale autoencoder structure of VAR (rewinding the feature map to a coarser scale by re-encoding the intermediate latent), and the side-by-side pseudocode in Fig. 4 makes the method very easy to understand and reproduce.

The empirical study of where to inject noise (CFG scheduling vs. text embedding vs. <SOS> token) is systematic and informative, and the Pareto-front analysis (Fig. 6) is a fair and appropriate way to evaluate a diversity-quality trade-off method rather than cherry-picking single operating points.

Experimental coverage is strong: two text-to-image VARs (Infinity, Switti), text-to-video (InfinityStar via VBench/VBench-2.0), class-conditioned VAR (suppl. H), comparisons against fine-tuning-based methods (CSD-VAR, Kaleido in suppl. I), robustness across CFG weights, temperature, nucleus sampling, and prompt-rewriting baselines, plus ablations on scale-travel parameters, model sizes/resolutions, and inference-time overhead (~15-24%), all of which support the claims.

The paper is well written and clearly organized; limitations are honestly stated (residual artifacts in ~6% of samples, slightly higher inference cost), and the text-alignment analysis (GenEval, VQAScore) addresses the natural concern that diversity gains come at the cost of prompt fidelity.
weaknesses: The diversity-enhancement component (condition-annealing via noise injection into the text embedding) is a direct transfer of CADS [68] from diffusion to VAR; the main novelty rests on scale-travel and the empirical finding of which injection target works best. The conceptual novelty is thus moderate, although the scale-axis adaptation is genuinely non-trivial.

Some results are internally mixed and could be discussed more carefully: e.g., in Tab. 1 condition-annealing alone improves FID over the baseline (15.53 vs. 19.16 for Infinity), and on MS-COCO FID for DiverseVAR (28.97) is worse than condition-annealing (22.51) on Infinity, which complicates the 'advancing the Pareto front' narrative on that metric; a per-metric operating-point justification would help.

Remaining quality cost is non-trivial: ImageReward drops by roughly 11-15% relative to the base models in Tab. 1, and text-alignment (GenEval, esp. Switti: 0.615 to 0.586; Color Attribution 0.368 to 0.333) degrades noticeably even if framed as insignificant. A human evaluation of the diversity-quality trade-off would strengthen the claims, but is absent.

Key experimental details are deferred to the supplementary (scheduler choices, hyperparameters, toy experiment for selecting 'optimal' settings); in particular, hyperparameter selection criteria for the main quantitative tables could bias the comparison between methods, and the paper would benefit from stating the selection protocol in the main text.

The scale-travel assumption that intermediate latents Z_l already encode global structure (relying on prior observations [33, 84]) means the method preserves coarse layout by design; this limits how much compositional diversity can be gained (qualitative results show mostly color/style/background variation), and the paper could discuss this ceiling on achievable diversity more explicitly.

Video evaluation applies DiverseVAR only to the keyframe stage of InfinityStar and uses augmented prompts in Fig. 7 (flagged with a dagger), which slightly weakens the end-to-end generality claim for video; the number of prompts (100 for Pareto curves) is also modest.
